extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science (readers studying theories of causation and laws of nature)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying conceptual criteria for what counts as a cause and for distinguishing causal laws from mere uniformities of phenomena in philosophy of science and inductive logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause as invariable and unconditional antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of a phenomenon is the antecedent, or the concurrence of antecedents, on which it is invariably and unconditionally consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unconditionalness (necessity) is essential: a sequence that is merely invariable in our experience but conditional on other antecedents (e.g., night followed by day) is not a cause. Example: the presence of a sufficiently luminous body (the sun) and absence of opaque medium are the sole conditions constituting the cause of day. Anti-pattern: treating an antecedent as cause when it is followed by the consequent only under additional conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause defined as assemblage of positive conditions (subject to only negative conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative convenient definition confines 'cause' to the assemblage of positive conditions without the negative: a cause is the assemblage of positive antecedents 'subject to no other than negative conditions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation emphasizes specifying the positive factors sufficient for the effect while allowing only absence-of-interference (negative conditions) as qualifications. Use when isolating a minimally sufficient set of antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariable sequence alone is insufficient for causation
rubrics_metrics.description: An observed uniform succession of two phenomena does not by itself establish causation unless the antecedent is the invariable antecedent (i.e., not merely conditionally invariable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: day and night have an invariable sequence in experience but are not cause-effect of one another because each can occur without the other if other antecedents (sun's position) differ. Do not infer causation solely from frequent succession without testing unconditionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for experimental/other evidence to show unconditionalness
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of a cause often depends on experimental grounds showing the antecedent would produce the consequent independently of the usual preceding conditions (experimentum crucis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: observation that when the sun is above the horizon there is daylight demonstrates experimentally that daylight follows from the sun rather than from the prior occurrence of night. Use experiments or observations that isolate antecedents to test whether the succession is unconditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Laws of Phenomena and investigation of causes (causes as more universal laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ascertainment of causes (causes which are themselves phenomena) is the ascertainment of other and more universal Laws of Phenomena; distinguishing general laws from contingent co-existences is essential to scientific inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a methodological distinction: investigating causes aims at more universal, explanatory generalizations, not merely cataloguing sequences. Beware conflating descriptive uniformities with explanatory causal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermixture of laws: composite antecedents produce conditional uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple unconditional causes co-exist, their co-existence can produce additional uniform sequences (intermixture of their laws) that are invariable while those causes co-exist but are not unconditional laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the combined effects of sun's attraction and Earth's motion produce a particular series of orbital motions that would change if either cause varied. Treat such composite uniformities as contingent on the continued co-existence of causes, not as independent causal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal relation: cause need not perceptibly precede effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a cause does not precede its effect in any observable interval in some cases, causation is the law of succession of phenomena; the beginning of a phenomenon implies a cause. When two co-existent phenomena are in doubt, determining which preceded the other solves cause/effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some effects may commence simultaneously with their causes (imperceptible intervals). Practical rule: if precedence can be ascertained between co-existent phenomena, the earlier is typically the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuance requirement: some effects need continued presence of cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions necessary for the first production of a phenomenon are occasionally also necessary for its continuance; more commonly continuity requires only negative conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mercury in an exhausted tube requires continued pressure to be sustained (needs continuing cause); a plowshare once made continues without continued heating. Distinguish instantaneous phenomena that must be continually reproduced from durable products that persist without active cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties/powers framework for heterogeneous effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same phenomenon yields heterogeneous simultaneous effects, each different sort of effect is attributed to a different 'property' or 'power' of the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concepts like gravitative, luminiferous, calorific properties to abridge and classify effects of a single cause. Note: these are convenient abstract names and do not themselves explain the connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent (primeval) causes versus derived phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist permanent natural agents (primeval causes) whose origin is inscrutable; all other phenomena are immediate or remote effects of these primeval causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we can give no account of the origin or distribution of primeval causes, co-existences among effects traceable to different primeval causes are treated as casual concurrences rather than unconditional laws. Do not infer universal co-existence of effects when they stem from contingently distributed primeval causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-existences among effects depend on identity or co-existence of their causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable co-existences among effects are results of either identity (same cause) or co-existence of their causes; there are no original, independent unconditional co-existences between effects of different causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only co-existences among properties of the same agent can claim law-like, unconditional status. Otherwise, treat co-existence as contingent on distribution of causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation/Persistence of Force as explanatory framework (empirical stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical findings show that different phenomena regarded as distinct sources of force (heat, electricity, chemical action, motion) are convertible into one another with definite, fixed quantitative equivalences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This empirical regularity allows treating many phenomena as manifestations of a single conserved magnitude and influences how we identify causal antecedents that account for transformations between modes (e.g., heat ↔ mechanical work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenditure or transfer of energy as a test for causation
rubrics_metrics.description: As a practical test for distinguishing causation from mere concomitance, if the effect consists in putting matter in motion then any antecedent object which has lost motion has contributed to the effect (transfer/expenditure of energy indicates causal contribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use energy transfer bookkeeping (per Mr. Bain) when applicable: if an antecedent's loss of motion accounts for the effect's motion, that antecedent is a causal contributor. This is a useful empirical sign but not a universal metaphysical definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause includes both force (changing antecedent) and collocation (stationary antecedents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assemblage constituting a cause must typically contain two elements: a force (a changing antecedent) and the collocation or positions of objects required for the force's particular effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to produce a bonfire you need fuel/air/spark (collocation) and the chemical action (force). When identifying causes, specify both the agent of change and the necessary configuration of objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potentiality vs actual motion: antecedent need not be actual motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Under conservation theories, antecedent 'force' may be potential rather than actual motion; the cause can be a collocation of objects possessing a property (potentiality of motion) rather than presently moving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that stored-up or potential energy (e.g., coal in the ground, stone on a height) functions as an antecedent property that can be the cause when appropriate collocation occurs (combustion, falling). Do not require actual motion at the antecedent moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminological/namely-usefulness of calling events 'causes'
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the term 'cause' to designate events/phenomena is a convenient generalization that needs involve no particular metaphysical theory, and provides a useful distinction in scientific discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rejecting the term for mere nomenclature reasons: it serves to mark fundamental distinctions necessary for framing a rigorous canon of induction and for communication in science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of extrapolating from local distributions of primeval causes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no means by which, from the distribution of primeval causes in one region of space, we could conjecture whether a similar distribution prevails elsewhere; thus sequences dependent on such distributions are not universally lawlike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution in generalizing co-existences observed locally to global laws when those co-existences depend on contingently distributed primeval agents.
